Radar absorbing materials absorb electromagnetic energy in specific radio wavelength ranges with minimal reflection.
RAM can be classified by composition and principle of action into resonance, non-resonant magnetic, metal screen, non-resonant bulk, and pyramidal absorbers.
Resonance RAM thickness corresponds to a quarter of the radar wavelength to achieve wave neutralization.
Ferrite particle size directly influences the effective absorption frequency, with smaller particles absorbing higher frequencies.
Nickel ferrites have high saturation magnetization and thermal stability but high initial losses.
Magnesium ferrites are used in the long-wave microwave range but have low thermal stability and induction values.
Metal screens consist of flat single or multi-layer plates providing shielding by reflection and absorption, effective mainly at low frequencies and normal incidence.
Non-resonant bulk RAM use thick layers combining dielectric and magnetic losses, often with graphite added to polyurethane foam.
Metamaterials exhibit negative magnetic permeability and electrical susceptibility, enabling unique electromagnetic wave interactions.
Metamaterial RAM use periodic lattices of Split Ring Resonators (SRRs) to absorb waves at plasma resonance frequencies.
Metamaterial RAM achieve absorption levels of at least 80% at 9.5 GHz for incidence angles up to 50 degrees.
Broadband absorption is challenging with traditional RAM due to narrow-band resonance and manufacturing difficulties.
The neutralization effect reduces reflected radar waves by destructive interference inside the RAM.
Ferrite-based RAM thickness is typically a few millimeters, offering flexibility but limited thermal stability.
Metal screen absorbers' effectiveness decreases with increasing frequency and off-normal wave incidence.

Radioabsorbing materials are used in anechoic chambers and stealth technology to mask radar signatures.
The absorption frequency range for ferrite particles varies from 0.5 GHz to 12 GHz depending on particle size.
Metamaterial RAM can be designed to have electrodynamic properties independent of wave polarization.
